of all that lives and breathes, he speaks only of the individual:
"What is now implied in the affirmation: I believe in God,
Father, Almighty, Creator ...?" Answer: "By this I mean
and believe that I am God's creation...
If this is so, then it is clear that belief in God as Creator
and belief in His wonder-working action and energy is not a
simple and easy matter, but a belief that is extremely difficult
and hardly possible to come by, and for that very reason it is
the fundamental thing. In fact belief in God as Creator
contains in essence the whole Christian faith. Luther says in
commenting on the creation story: "For doubtless the most
important article of the faith is that in which we declare: I
believe in God, Father Omnipotent, Creator of heaven and
earth. And whoever truly believes this, has already been
helped and restored to the right way and has reached the
state from which Adam fell. But there are few people who
have progressed so far as to believe in the fullest sense that
our God is the God who creates and makes all things."1
"There are few such"! Do we belong to these few? Are we
in truth constantly aware that we are God's creation? Does
the unfolding course of events in world history always strike
us as being grounded in the wondrous activity of God?
We may well no doubt have moments such as those we
mentioned earlier in which we believe we see the miracles
which God effects. But do these moments give light to our
whole life, so that we always realize ourselves to be held in
God's creator hand? Nay, do they retain their sway when our
passions overwhelm us or when we are struck by a fate which
threatens to break us utterly? The beautiful and uplifting
things we have experienced may well sound a comforting
echo and prove a precious possession in times of hardship
and distress. But can we hold on to them in hours of cruel
pain and bitterest renunciation and sacrifice? Do they suffice
to make us always certain of God as the Creator of all things?
